I recently graduated from UC Berkeley with my BS (with Highest Honors) and MS in EECS! I was not alone in this journey, and I have many people to thank: As I learned in my first semester, Berkeley is a fantastic place for research, and I am very grateful to the professors and mentors who supported me. I enjoyed working on machine learning and genomics with Professor Nilah Ioannidis and Ruchir Rastogi , student-AI tutor interactions with Narges Norouzi , and AI agents that summarize news with Serina Chang . Special thank you to my Master’s advisor Gireeja Ranade as we worked on studying alignment challenges in educational AI. I am also grateful to the Siebel Scholars Program and Mark Asta for recognizing me as a Siebel Scholar and for supporting me financially during my Master’s. I also spent eight semesters serving as a TA for EECS16A, CS61B, and CS188. These experiences, particularly my three semesters as head TA, showed me how much effort it takes to run a 500+ student course—and how seeing students’ progress makes it all worth it. Thank you to numerous faculty who trusted me in these positions, including Dan Klein , Stuart Russell , Emma Pierson , Peyrin Kao, Josh Hug , and Justin Yokota . One highlight: getting to give a guest lecture in CS61B on collaboration in software engineering! Living at Bowles Hall Residential College with Gasper Begus and antje postema taught me what it means to live as a community and exposed me to a wide variety of ways of thinking across disciplines. I especially enjoyed getting to advise younger students academically, professionally, and socially as an Undergraduate Fellow. Finally, a load of thanks to the friends who made my grueling Berkeley experience so fun, and to my family for their unwavering support since day one. Graduation is always bittersweet, and while I will miss being a student at Berkeley, I look forward to this next chapter where I can now give back to the university. Go Bears!

Today, I'm announcing Cold Start: a series where I uncover the unscalable growth strategies brought companies 0 → 1. Most founders today start with a built-in advantage: an ex-apple employee, an ex-VC investor, or an ex-founder. But the rest of us do not. From selling cereal boxes to stay alive, making handmade gift boxes to land early customers, to converting sororities into users. My goal is to tell the stories of those who started without one. Last Wednesday, I had the amazing opportunity to participate in Jane Street 's WiSE Program in NYC. I enjoyed learning about their work, previewing the office, and meeting fellow math/CS enthusiasts, including MIT beavers. Huge thank you to Katie Nasta and Kylie Newman for organizing the program; it was a fantastic introduction to Jane Street and quantitative finance! Afterward, I flew back to SF Friday night to make it to Y Combinator 's Startup School 2026, where I met so many talented founders and builders. One key takeaway from the conference was the importance of working on ideas you have conviction in (especially those that conventional wisdom would advise against, because they have the most potential). And, in the AI age, if there was ever a time to found a startup, it’s now. It was inspiring to meet and hear from Vivian Midha Shen , founder of Acely AI and Gunn High School alum, among other incredible tech executives and leaders. Looking forward to using my 6 free months of Claude Max 20x (while realizing product overhang and unhobbling Claude, thanks to advice from Boris Cherny ). Grateful for an amazing week!

Spent the weekend in San Francisco for Y Combinator Startup School. Really enjoyed hearing from keynote speakers Jensen Huang , Sam Altman, Boris Cherny , Alexandr Wang , checking out some impressive demos, and meeting a bunch of ambitious people. Also convinced a group of strangers to get ice cream with us. If you were part of the ice cream gang, say hi!

Last week, I finished my internship at Microsoft as a Machine Learning Engineer Intern. This summer, I worked in Microsoft Teams and built a fully on-device machine learning system for real-time voice interaction. My work focused on designing a low-latency pipeline that integrates speech recognition, LLM-based reasoning, and speech synthesis: enabling fast, reliable, and private user experiences without relying on the cloud and significantly reducing cost. I focused on building low-latency ML systems by designing LLM routing pipelines, creating synthetic datasets for evaluation, fine-tuning models with methods like LoRA, and exploring local vs. cloud inference tradeoffs. This project pushed me to think deeply about systems design, model performance, and real-world deployment constraints while navigating real-world tradeoffs between performance, efficiency, and reliability in production systems. Huge thank you to my team and mentors for their guidance and support, especially my manager Ashish Mehta, mentor Prayank Mathur , and my interviewer Eli Kravez . I’m incredibly grateful for the opportunity to work on such impactful problems at scale. I’m also grateful to the other interns that I met during my internship for making this such an amazing experience and I’m looking forward to starting my 5th Year Masters program and utilizing the skills I learned this summer. #microsoft #internship

Spent this weekend at YC Startup School, and it was easily one of the most inspiring events I've been to. I met so many talented builders from schools like Duke, UIUC, Yale, UCLA, and more. It was exciting hearing about everything people were building, from diffusion models and AI agents in healthcare to robotics and developer tools. One of the highlights was hearing Chelsea Finn and Jensen Huang speak. Listening to their perspectives on the future of AI made me even more excited to keep building in this space. Really grateful for the opportunity, the conversations, and all the people I met this weekend. Looking forward to seeing what everyone builds next!
